# How to use these editorials

Each block is an original derivation, not a substitute for attempting the
linked task. Read the restatement only to compare your interpretation. Then
look for the recognition signal, reproduce the proof route, and finally check
the implementation traps. For external problems, the course teaches the tools;
these notes teach why that particular statement calls for them.

# 1. 71A -- Way Too Long Words

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/71/A>

## Restatement and recognition

Transform each independent word according to one length threshold. There is no
interaction between cases, so the correct model is a direct input/output loop,
not a string algorithm.

## Algorithm, proof, and tests

For a word `s`, leave it unchanged when `len(s) <= 10`; otherwise output
`s[0]`, `len(s)-2`, and `s.back()`. The two branches partition all legal word
lengths. In the long branch, exactly the first and last characters are kept,
so the count between them is exactly `len(s)-2`; therefore the output matches
the requested abbreviation. The time is `O(total input characters)`.

Test lengths 1, 10, 11, and 100. In C++, concatenate `string` and
`to_string`; in Python use an f-string. Do not treat the threshold as `>= 10`.

# 2. 4C -- Registration System

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/4/C>

## State meaning

Maintain `next[name]`: the smallest suffix not yet suggested for this base
name, with zero meaning that the unsuffixed name has never appeared. On a new
base name, print `OK` and set `next[name] = 1`. Otherwise print
`name + next[name]` and increment it.

## Why no extra occupied-name set is needed

The requests themselves are lowercase base names, while every generated suffix
for one base is issued in increasing order. Once suffix `t` is printed, all
smaller positive suffixes for that base were printed earlier, and `t+1` is the
next free one. The map invariant therefore yields the smallest allowed suffix.
Expected time is `O(total name length)` with a hash map, and memory is linear
in the distinct requested names.

Test the same base three times, two interleaved bases, and a request that looks
like another generated name. Use `unordered_map<string,int>` or `dict`; never
scan suffixes from 1 on every duplicate.

# 3. 363B -- Fence

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/363/B>

## Observation

Every candidate is a fixed-length window. After computing the first sum, moving
the window one step removes exactly its leftmost height and adds exactly its new
rightmost height.

## Algorithm and proof

Set `sum = a[0] + ... + a[k-1]`, remember it as the current best, and for each
right endpoint `r >= k` update `sum += a[r] - a[r-k]`. Compare the resulting
window `[r-k+1, r]` to the best. By induction, just before each comparison
`sum` equals the sum of that window: it is true initially, and the update
removes/adds precisely the changed elements. Every length-`k` window appears
once, so the minimum remembered sum is globally minimum. Time `O(n)`, memory
`O(1)` besides input.

Output the stored left endpoint plus one. Test `k=1`, `k=n`, and equal window
sums; the problem accepts any minimizer, but your comparison decides the tie.

# 4. 279B -- Books

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/279/B>

## Invariant

All reading times are positive. Keep a window `[l,r]` with sum at most `t`
after repeatedly advancing `l` while it is too expensive. Then it is the
longest feasible window ending at `r`: moving `l` farther right only shortens
it, and moving it left would violate the budget.

## Algorithm, proof, and complexity

Extend `r` from left to right and add `a[r]`. While the sum exceeds `t`, remove
`a[l++]`. Maximize `r-l+1`. The invariant above proves each recorded length is
feasible and no feasible window ending at `r` is longer. Each endpoint advances
at most `n` times, yielding `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra memory.

The positivity is essential: with negative times, a removed prefix could later
become useful and this proof fails. Test a single over-budget book, an exact
budget, and an optimal window beginning after index zero.

# 5. 158B -- Taxi

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/158/B>

## Forced greedy packing

Count groups of sizes 1, 2, 3, 4. Every size-4 group is alone. Every size-3
group must occupy a taxi and can take at most one size-1 group, so pair those
first. Pair size-2 groups together; one remaining size-2 can take up to two
ones. Finally pack remaining ones four per taxi.

## Proof route

The size-3 decision is forced: no group other than a one can share its taxi,
so using a one there cannot hurt a future fuller packing. Size-2 groups only
fit with another size-2 or ones; pairing twos maximizes the remaining capacity
for ones. After those forced classes, only ones remain, and four per taxi is
optimal by capacity. Thus the construction uses the minimum possible taxis.

All operations are `O(n)`. Test no ones for size-3 groups, an odd number of
twos, and one/two/three/four leftover ones. Do not simulate individual taxis.

# 6. 706B -- Interesting Drink

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/706/B>

## Recognition and algorithm

The same static set of prices serves many threshold queries. Sort it once. For
a budget `x`, the answer is the first index strictly greater than `x`, namely
`upper_bound(prices.begin(), prices.end(), x) - prices.begin()` in C++ or
`bisect_right(prices, x)` in Python.

## Correctness and traps

Sorting places every price `<= x` before every price `> x`; the first position
after the former group is therefore exactly their count. Preprocessing costs
`O(n log n)` and each query `O(log n)`. Test a budget below every price, equal
to duplicate prices, and above every price. `lower_bound` counts `< x` and is
wrong at equality.

# 7. 520B -- Two Buttons

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/520/B>

## State graph

An integer is a vertex, and each button press is a unit-cost directed edge.
BFS finds the fewest presses once the state space is bounded. If `n >= m`, only
decrementing is useful, so answer `n-m`. Otherwise no optimal route needs to
visit a value above `2m`: after first exceeding `m`, a decrement-only suffix
reaches `m`; overshooting past `2m` cannot beat stopping at or below `2m`.

## Algorithm and proof

Run BFS on `[0, 2m]` from `n`, visiting `x-1` when nonnegative and `2x` when
within the bound. BFS explores paths by increasing length, so its first visit
to `m` is optimal. The bound argument ensures an optimal path is represented.
Time and memory are `O(m)` in the `n<m` branch.

Test `n=m`, `n>m`, `m=1`, and a case where doubling first is worse than a
decrement. Mark visited when enqueuing, not when dequeuing.

# 8. 455A -- Boredom

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/455/A>

## Compress the story by value

Choosing value `x` eventually earns `gain[x] = x * frequency[x]`; taking all
copies is always at least as good as taking fewer. It forbids only neighboring
values. Thus `dp[x]` is the best score using values at most `x`.

```text
dp[x] = max(dp[x-1], dp[x-2] + gain[x])
```

## Correctness and implementation

An optimal solution either omits `x`, giving `dp[x-1]`, or takes it, forcing
the rest to use values at most `x-2`, giving the second term. These exhaustive,
disjoint cases prove the recurrence by induction. Sweep through the maximum
input value using two rolling `long long` states. Complexity is `O(max value +
n)` time and `O(max value)` memory for frequencies.

Test repeated equal values, values separated by gaps, and a choice where one
large frequency beats a neighboring value. Do not sort individual occurrences
and apply the recurrence to positions; the conflict is between values.

# 9. 300C -- Beautiful Numbers

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/300/C>

## Count by number of `a` digits

If exactly `i` positions contain digit `a`, the digit sum is
`s = i*a + (n-i)*b`, and there are `C(n,i)` strings with that composition.
Check whether every decimal digit of `s` is either `a` or `b`; if so, add the
binomial coefficient.

## Proof and complexity

Every legal string has one unique `i`, and all strings with that `i` have the
same digit sum. The digit check selects exactly the legal compositions, while
the binomial coefficient counts their distinct position choices. Precompute
factorials and inverse factorials modulo the prime, using Fermat's inverse.
The work is `O(n + number of digits checked across n+1 sums)`, effectively
`O(n log n)`.

The input guarantees `1 <= a < b <= 9`, so the digit sum is positive. Test
`a=1, b=9`, a sum containing a forbidden interior digit, and a composition
where only one value of `i` succeeds. Use modular arithmetic only for counts,
never for the decimal digit sum.

# 10. 166B -- Polygons

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/166/B>

## Reduce containment to convex point location

Because A is convex, if every vertex of B is strictly inside A, every edge and
every interior point of B is also inside A: they are convex combinations of
points of A's interior. Thus test every B vertex against A. For one point P,
use `A[0]` as a fan pivot. First reject P unless it is strictly between rays
`A[0]->A[1]` and `A[0]->A[n-1]`; then binary-search the fan sector
`(A[0], A[i], A[i+1])` containing P and require strict inclusion in that
triangle using cross-product signs.

## Why this is sufficient

A convex polygon is partitioned by its pivot fan into triangles. The ray tests
select a unique possible sector, and the triangle test is equivalent to strict
membership in that sector. Therefore every accepted B vertex is strictly in A.
Convexity then proves the whole of B is inside; any rejected vertex proves it
is not. The time is `O(m log n)` and memory is `O(1)` beyond the polygons.

Use `long long` for cross products. Test clockwise input, an inner vertex on
A's edge, a B edge that comes close to A, and a point just beyond one fan
boundary. Never use floating point.

# 11. 20C -- Dijkstra?

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/20/C>

## Model and algorithm

All edge weights are positive, so Dijkstra applies. Store `dist[v]` and
`parent[v]`; on a strict relaxation of `u -> v`, set `parent[v]=u`. Use a
min-heap of `(distance, vertex)` pairs and ignore stale entries. If `n` remains
infinite, print `-1`; otherwise follow parents from `n` to 1 and reverse.

## Correctness proof

When Dijkstra extracts a non-stale vertex, no unexplored path can improve it:
such a path first crosses from an extracted prefix through a nonnegative edge,
so it cannot arrive cheaper. Thus every relaxation uses a correct shortest
prefix. A parent is assigned only when an edge creates the current best
distance, so following parents reconstructs a shortest path to vertex 1.
Complexity is `O((n+m) log n)`.

Test disconnected graphs, parallel edges, and a route whose first discovered
path is later improved. Distances need `long long`; a boolean `visited` on heap
insertion would incorrectly freeze an improvable vertex.

# 12. 161D -- Distance in Tree

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/161/D>

## Bounded-depth tree DP

Root the tree. Let `cnt[u][d]` be the number of vertices in `u`'s subtree at
distance `d` from `u`, for `0 <= d <= k`; initialize `cnt[u][0]=1`. Process a
child `v` after its table is ready. Before merging it, every pair with one end
in the accumulated part of `u` and the other in `v` contributes when
`d1 + d2 + 1 = k`.

## Merge, proof, and complexity

For each child and each `0 <= d < k`, add
`cnt[v][d] * cnt[u][k-d-1]` to the answer, then shift `cnt[v][d]` into
`cnt[u][d+1]`. Every pair has a unique lowest common ancestor; it is counted
exactly when the second relevant child subtree merges there. No pair in one
child is recounted because that child already handled it. The bounded
`k <= 500` gives `O(nk)` time and memory.

Test a path, a star, `k=1`, and `k` larger than the diameter. Count in
`long long`; merge cross-pairs before shifting the child table.

# 13. 580D -- Kefa and Dishes

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/580/D>

## State captures the only relevant history

Use `dp[mask][last]`: maximum satisfaction for exactly the dishes in `mask`
ordered with `last` final. Append an unused dish `next`:

```text
dp[mask | bit(next)][next] = max(current,
                                 dp[mask][last] + base[next] + bonus[last][next])
```

Start each one-dish mask with its base value, and maximize states with
`popcount(mask)=m`.

## Proof and costs

The future bonus depends only on the final dish and the used set; earlier order
details have already contributed their adjacent bonuses. Inductively, each
transition appends every possible final dish to every valid shorter ordering,
so the table considers every legal ordered selection exactly by its best value.
There are `2^n * n` states and `O(2^n n^2)` transitions.

Test asymmetric bonuses, `m=1`, and a bonus that makes a lower-base dish worth
choosing. The common wrong state is `dp[mask]`: it loses the predecessor needed
to price the next append.

# 14. 1245D -- Shichikuji and Power Grid

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1245/D>

## Virtual-source reduction

Create vertex 0. Edge `(0,i)` means build a station in city `i`, with the
given station cost. Edge `(i,j)` means wire the two cities, with the supplied
Manhattan-based cost. Any plan that powers all cities corresponds to a connected
subgraph containing 0, and vice versa. The minimum plan is therefore an MST.

## Algorithm and proof

Generate all `O(n^2)` city edges plus source edges and run Kruskal, recording
source edges as stations and the others as wires. An MST is no heavier than any
connected subgraph because removing cycles never disconnects it or increases
cost. The correspondence proves its output is an optimal power plan. With
`n <= 2000`, `O(n^2 log n)` is acceptable.

Use 64-bit costs. Test that a very expensive station is replaced by a wire, that
two cheap stations remain separate, and that positive coordinates have a large
Manhattan difference.

# 15. 271D -- Good Substrings

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/271/D>

## Enumerate starts, identify contents exactly

The length limit permits `O(n^2)` substring enumeration. For each start,
extend the end while maintaining the bad-character count; stop once it exceeds
`k`. Insert the traversed characters into a trie. A trie node represents one
unique prefix from the root and hence one unique substring; creating a node
counts a new distinct valid substring. With at most `n(n+1)/2` nodes and 26
lowercase transitions per node, an `array<int,26>` trie fits the stated 512 MB
limit in C++ at `n=1500`.

## Correctness and testing

The maintained bad count is exactly the count in the current extension, so the
loop inserts every and only valid occurrences. Equal contents follow the same
trie edges and end at the same node; distinct contents diverge at their first
different character and end at different nodes. Thus the created-node count is
exactly the desired number. Work is `O(n^2)` time and `O(n^2 * alphabet)`
integer storage in the fixed-alphabet implementation.

Test repeated characters, all-good/all-bad masks, `k=0`, and repeated equal
substrings from different starts. Do not insert `(start,end)`: that counts
occurrences, not distinct strings. A double hash is a smaller-memory optional
Python strategy, but it is probabilistic and is not the proof-backed default.

# 16. 61E -- Enemy Is Weak

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/61/E>

## Split each decreasing triple at its middle

For each `j`, multiply the number of earlier values greater than `a[j]` by the
number of later values smaller than `a[j]`. Sum the products. Coordinate
compress values; a Fenwick tree scans left-to-right for earlier counts, and a
second scan right-to-left obtains later counts.

## Proof and complexity

Every valid triple has one unique middle index `j`, and choosing either valid
endpoint is independent once `a[j]` is fixed. Thus the product counts exactly
the triples centered at `j`, with no overlap between different middles. Fenwick
updates and prefix queries make the time `O(n log n)` and memory `O(n)`.

For duplicates, strict comparisons require `seen - prefix(rank)` and
`prefix(rank-1)`; this task gives distinct values, but writing the strict forms
prevents a bad habit. Test sorted increasing, sorted decreasing, and `n<3`.

# 17. 86D -- Powerful Array

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/86/D>

## Maintain the statistic while moving a range

Order queries by Mo blocks. Keep `freq[x]` and current answer
`sum x * freq[x]^2`. Adding value `x` changes its contribution from
`x*f^2` to `x*(f+1)^2`; remove the old contribution, increment, and add the
new one. Removal is the reverse. Move `L` and `R` one step at a time to each
next query, then store the current answer at its original query index.

## Why it works

The invariant is exact: `freq` represents precisely the current interval and
the answer is the sum of each value's contribution from those frequencies. Each
primitive move preserves it by replacing only the changed value's term. Mo
ordering changes visit order, not query contents, so each saved answer is
correct. Typical complexity is `O((n+q) sqrt(n))` moves with `O(n)` memory.

Use `long long`. Test repeated one value, moving both endpoints backward, and
queries returned in a different order than their sorted processing order.

# 18. 498C -- Array and Operations

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/498/C>

## Decompose operations by prime

Factor every number. Fix a prime `p`: each exponent at an odd-index vertex is
supply, each exponent at an even-index vertex is demand, and each allowed
odd-even pair is an infinite-capacity edge. The maximum number of `p`-units
removed is a max flow. Sum independently over all primes that occur.

## Reduction proof

Any allowed division by a composite can be split into one operation per prime
factor on the same pair. This preserves feasibility and increases (or at least
preserves) the number of counted operations, so some optimum uses prime-only
operations. A flow unit travels from an odd exponent through an allowed pair to
an even exponent, exactly representing one removable common prime unit.
Capacities prevent using an exponent unit twice. Conversely every sequence of
prime-unit operations yields such a flow. Therefore max flow equals the optimum
count for that prime, and primes do not interact. Factorization plus Dinic per
occurring prime is feasible for `n,m <= 100`.

Normalize each pair orientation by index parity. Test no shared prime, one
large repeated prime exponent, and a path where flow must choose between two
neighbors.

# 19. 319C -- Kalila and Dimna in the Logging Industry

Official: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/319/C>

## Derive lines before choosing a hull

The recurrence has form

```text
dp[i] = min over j < i of (dp[j] + b[j] * a[i])
```

For fixed `j`, this is the line `y = b[j] * x + dp[j]` queried at `x=a[i]`.
The base case is `dp[1]=0`: insert line `y=b[1]x` before querying for `i=2`.
After computing `dp[i]`, insert `y=b[i]x+dp[i]`. The stated monotonicity gives
query `a[i]` values increasing and slopes `b[j]` decreasing, so a monotone
lower hull with a moving query pointer works; a Li Chao tree is a robust
alternative.

## Hull invariant and proof

Keep candidate lines in slope order. When a new line makes the intersection of
the last two candidates lie no later than the prior intersection, the middle
line is never minimal for any future increasing query and can be removed. The
front pointer advances only while its successor is no worse at the current
query. Thus the queried line is minimum among all inserted lines, which equals
the recurrence minimum by induction. The monotone hull runs in `O(n)` time;
Li Chao gives `O(n log coordinate range)`.

Use cross multiplication with wide integers for redundancy tests, avoiding
floating point. Test equal-looking line values at a query, a line optimal only
for a short interval, and values near `10^9`.

# 20. 786B -- Legacy

## Reduction

An interval edge is not one edge: expanding it naively can be quadratic. Build
two segment-tree graphs. An "out" tree has zero-cost edges from a parent to its
children, so one vertex can reach every leaf in an interval through `O(log n)`
nodes. An "in" tree reverses those zero-cost edges, so every leaf in an
interval can reach one vertex through `O(log n)` nodes. Connect the original
vertex to the canonical out-tree cover, or the in-tree cover to the original
vertex, with the requested weight. Dijkstra on this expanded nonnegative graph
is then ordinary shortest path. Prove both directions: every range operation
has a zero-cost tree route plus exactly one weighted edge, and every such route
represents an allowed range operation.

# 21. 191C -- Fools and Roads

## Tree difference invariant

Root the tree. For a path `(u,v)`, add one at `u` and `v`, subtract two at
`lca(u,v)`. Process vertices in postorder, adding each child's accumulated
value into its parent. The final value stored at a child equals the number of
query paths crossing that child's parent edge: a path contributes one net unit
to exactly the two branches leaving its LCA. This turns all paths into `O(1)`
updates plus LCA queries. Use binary lifting and 64-bit counts.

# 22. 208E -- Blood Cousins

## Lift, group by depth, count an interval

Find the `p`-th ancestor `a` of `v` by binary lifting. All requested cousins
are exactly vertices at `depth[v]` inside `a`'s subtree. A DFS gives every
subtree a contiguous entry-time interval; for every depth, store sorted entry
times of vertices at that depth. Two binary searches count that depth list
inside `[tin[a], tout[a]]`, then subtract one for `v`. If the ancestor does not
exist, the answer is zero. The definition, rather than the family story, is
what makes the reduction precise.

# 23. 375D -- Tree and Queries

## Keep the heavy subtree's frequency table

Use DSU on tree. Solve light children with a cleared frequency table, solve the
heavy child and keep its table, then add every vertex of each light subtree.
Maintain `count[color]` and a second frequency-of-frequencies structure so a
query asks how many colors have count at least `k`. The heavy child is kept
because every vertex is rebuilt only for light-edge ancestors, giving
`O(n log n)` additions. The important invariant is that the maintained table
contains exactly the current subtree when its query is answered.

# 24. 600E -- Lomsat gelral

## Small-to-large maps

For each subtree, keep a frequency map and the current largest frequency plus
the sum of colors achieving it. Merge the smaller child's map into the larger
map; when a color's count rises, update the maximum and sum carefully. Every
map entry moves only into a map at least twice as large, so total map work is
`O(n log n)` expected with hash maps. The answer for a vertex is read after all
children are merged. Reset the sum when a strictly larger frequency appears.

# 25. 877E -- Danil and a Part-time Job

## Euler-tour range toggles

An Euler tour maps every subtree to one contiguous interval. A segment tree
stores the number of ones in an interval; a lazy flip turns a segment sum `s`
into `length - s` and toggles one lazy bit. Range flip and range sum are then
standard. The lazy flag means "every value under this node has been inverted an
odd number of times not yet pushed"; applying a second flip cancels it. Test
two flips of the same subtree and a leaf.

# 26. 242E -- XOR on Segment

## Store bit counts, not only the sum

For every segment and bit position, store how many values have that bit set.
The segment sum is the weighted sum of these counts. Xoring a mask flips every
selected bit, replacing its count by `length - count`; the mask is therefore a
lazy tag combined by xor. A plain range sum cannot be updated after xor because
carry interactions hide which bits changed. The bit-count representation makes
each flipped bit independent. Use enough bits for the stated value range.

# 27. 103D -- Time to Raid Cowavans

## Split queries by step size

For small step `b`, precompute suffix-style sums `dp[i][b] = a[i] +
dp[i+b][b]`; each query is then `O(1)`. For large `b`, directly jump through
the array, which takes only `O(n / b)` positions. Choose a threshold near
`sqrt(n)`: precomputation costs `O(n sqrt(n))`, and every large-step query is
also `O(sqrt(n))`. This is a standard time-memory tradeoff; indexing must match
the problem's one-based positions.

# 28. 1000F -- One Occurrence

## Sweep by right endpoint

When processing a right endpoint `r`, record for each value its latest and
previous occurrence. A value is unique in `[l,r]` exactly when its latest
occurrence is at least `l` and its previous occurrence is before `l`. Maintain
at the latest position a score equal to its previous occurrence, removing the
old latest position when the value repeats. A segment tree over positions can
find any position in `[l,r]` whose score is below `l`. Answer queries sorted by
right endpoint. The score is a compact certificate of uniqueness.

# 29. 240F -- TorCoder

## Count letters, then rebuild the range

Use 26 segment trees or one tree storing a 26-entry frequency vector. Query a
range's counts, clear each letter count in that range, then assign contiguous
blocks back in alphabetic or reverse-alphabetic order. Lazy assignment tags are
better than moving characters one by one: assigning a node to one letter sets
one count to its length and all others to zero. The queried multiset is
preserved and the reconstructed blocks are exactly its sorted order. The factor
26 is constant.

# 30. 343D -- Water Tree

## One tree, two interval families

Euler order makes a subtree one interval. Heavy-light decomposition makes a
root-to-vertex path a logarithmic number of intervals. Store binary fill state
in a lazy segment tree supporting range assignment to zero or one and point
query. Filling a subtree is one Euler interval; emptying a path is a sequence
of HLD intervals. Assignment tags overwrite prior assignments, which matches
the operation semantics. Keep the two coordinate systems distinct in your
proof: both refer to the same base-array positions.

# 31. 1209E2 -- Rotate Columns

## Keep only useful columns, then subset DP

Only the largest few columns can matter: a selected value for any row must be
among the strongest candidates for that row, so retain at most `n` promising
columns. For one retained column, try every rotation and compute, for every row
subset, the best sum this column can contribute to that subset. DP over row
masks combines columns, assigning each row once. The state is small because
the row count is small; the large column count is removed before DP. Verify the
rotation is chosen once per column, not separately per row.

# 32. 1416C -- XOR Inverse

## Decide each xor bit independently

Build a binary trie recursively over value bits. At one bit, all cross-pairs
between the zero and one groups have their relative order determined by whether
the corresponding bit of `x` is zero or one. Count inversions for both choices
while recursively solving inside groups; lower bits cannot affect pairs already
separated at this bit. Choose the cheaper option independently and set that bit
of `x` accordingly. The divide proof is lexicographic: the highest differing
bit decides an inversion before any lower bit is examined.

# 33. 13E -- Holes

## Sqrt-decompose jump chains

Divide indices into blocks. For every position, precompute the first position
outside its block reached by repeatedly jumping, the number of jumps needed,
and the last in-block position. A query follows only block exits, so it visits
`O(sqrt n)` blocks. After a point update, recompute its block backward because
each precomputed state depends only on later positions in that block. This is
faster than recomputing all jump paths and avoids recursion depth issues.

# 34. 342E -- Xenia and Tree

## Centroid ancestors summarize red updates

Build a centroid decomposition. For every original vertex, keep its list of
centroid ancestors and distances to them. A red update at `v` minimizes
`best[centroid]` with that distance along all its centroid ancestors. A query
at `u` minimizes `best[c] + dist(u,c)` over `u`'s centroid ancestors. Any path
from a queried vertex to a red vertex meets at their relevant centroid split,
which makes this summary complete. Both operations are `O(log n)`.

# 35. 895C -- Square Subsets

## Parity masks of prime exponents

The product is a square exactly when every prime exponent is even. Factor each
bounded value into a bitmask of exponent parities. DP over masks counts ways to
choose processed values; selecting a value xors its mask. Equal values are
grouped, and their even/odd subset counts multiply transitions efficiently.
Value one has mask zero but still doubles subset choices, so handle it
carefully. Subtract the empty subset from the final zero-mask count.

# 36. 868F -- Yet Another Minimization Problem

## Divide-and-conquer DP with a movable cost window

Let `dp[g][i]` be the minimum cost to partition the first `i` values into `g`
segments. Its transition minimizes `dp[g-1][j] + cost(j+1,i)`. The optimal
split points are monotone for this cost, enabling divide-and-conquer
optimization. Maintain `cost(l,r)` with two pointers and frequency counts: when
adding a value with current frequency `f`, it creates `f` new equal pairs.
Compute each DP row recursively over index intervals with narrowed candidate
split ranges. Prove the monotonicity theorem before applying this optimization.

# 37. 1292C -- Xenon's Attack on the Gangs

## DP on ordered endpoint pairs

Root the tree once for subtree sizes. For an ordered pair `(u,v)`, move `u`
toward `v` and move `v` toward `u`; the removed-side component sizes form the
current product, while future choices reduce one endpoint path at a time.
Memoize the best product reachable from each pair. The recursion terminates as
their distance decreases. LCA and binary lifting identify the child on a path,
so each transition knows the relevant component size. Do not confuse subtree
size with the component on the opposite side of an edge.

# 38. 613D -- Kingdom and its Cities

## Virtual tree preserves only relevant ancestry

Sort marked vertices by DFS entry time, add LCAs of adjacent marked vertices,
and connect them with a stack to form the virtual tree. Every path interaction
between marked vertices occurs on this compressed tree; unrelated original
vertices only form edge lengths. A bottom-up DP decides whether a virtual-tree
node carries an unresolved marked requirement or must be removed. If a marked
vertex has a marked parent adjacent in the virtual tree with no removable
vertex between them, report impossibility. Building and solving the virtual
tree is `O(k log k)` per query.

# 39. 1110F -- Nearest Leaf

## Reroot distances as range additions

Euler-order leaves so each subtree is an interval. For a fixed query vertex,
distances to leaves can be represented in a segment tree over that order. When
rerooting across an edge of weight `w`, distances to leaves inside the child's
subtree decrease by `w` while all other leaf distances increase by `w`; these
are lazy range additions. DFS carries this representation, answers interval
minimum queries, and undoes updates on return. The invariant is that the tree
stores distance from the current DFS root to every leaf.

# 40. 587C -- Duff in the Army

## Merge only the smallest needed identifiers

Precompute binary-lifting ancestors. Alongside every jump, store the sorted
list of its smallest at most ten person identifiers. Merge two such lists by a
two-pointer merge truncated to ten. Decompose a path through its LCA and merge
the stored lists of its upward jumps, including the LCA's local people. Larger
identifiers can be discarded because a query never asks for more than the fixed
limit. This truncation is the key state-compression proof.

# 41. 786C -- Till I Collapse

## Divide answer values by their first segment endpoint

For a fixed `k`, greedy segmentation is optimal because extending a segment
until the next item would introduce a `(k+1)`-st distinct value leaves the
longest possible first segment. Computing this independently for all `k` is
too slow. Use divide and conquer over `k` values: evaluate a midpoint greedily
with a data structure that finds the next position where distinct-count exceeds
the limit, then use monotonicity of segment endpoints/counts to restrict work.
The implementation is demanding; first prove why the greedy partition is
unique in its earliest-cut form.

# 42. 1093G -- Multidimensional Queries

## Manhattan distance is a maximum over sign masks

For points `p,q`, `|p-q|_1` equals the maximum over all `2^d` sign vectors of
`sign dot p - sign dot q`. Store for every segment-tree node the minimum and
maximum projection for every sign mask. Merge nodes componentwise; a query's
answer is the maximum `max[mask] - min[mask]`. Point updates rebuild one leaf
and its ancestors. With `d <= 5`, the mask factor is small and exact.

# 43. 321E -- Ciel and Gondolas

## Prefix costs plus monotone divide-and-conquer DP

Precompute every group cost from two-dimensional prefix sums. Let `dp[g][i]`
be the best cost for the first `i` people in `g` groups. The recurrence tries
the last cut `j`; the problem's quadrangle/Monge structure makes optimal cuts
monotone as `i` grows. Divide-and-conquer computes a DP row while searching
only the inherited cut interval. The common bug is counting each pair twice:
derive the exact group-cost formula against a two-person example first.

# 44. 896C -- Willem, Chtholly and Seniorious

## Ordered disjoint intervals, with stated randomness assumptions

Keep maximal equal-value intervals in an ordered map. Split intervals at query
boundaries, operate on whole intervals, then merge adjacent equal intervals
when appropriate. Assignment replaces a range by one interval; addition changes
each covered interval; kth and power-sum scan the interval multiset. This is an
ordered-disjoint-tree technique whose practical complexity relies on the
problem's pseudorandom operations, not a universal worst-case guarantee. Do not
use it when adversarial updates are possible.

# 45. 833B -- The Bakery

## Divide-and-conquer DP with dynamic distinct cost

The recurrence is `dp[g][i] = max_j dp[g-1][j] + distinct(j+1,i)`. Maintain
the distinct count of a moving interval using last occurrences: when extending
the right endpoint, the score changes according to whether that value was
already present. The required optimization proves monotonicity of optimal cut
positions, then computes each row by divide and conquer while moving the cost
window. This is the maximization counterpart of the previous segmentation DP;
write the exact interval convention before coding.

# 46. 311B -- Cats Transport

## Remove station travel before partitioning waiting times

Convert every cat's arrival to its effective time at the final station by
subtracting its station's prefix travel distance. Sort these values. If one bus
serves a consecutive group, its best departure time is the last effective
arrival in that group, making group cost a prefix-sum expression. The remaining
problem is partition DP with monotone optimal cuts, solved by divide and
conquer optimization. The reduction from physical stations to effective times
is the important modeling step.

# 47. 55D -- Beautiful Numbers

## Digit DP over divisibility state

Every nonzero decimal digit divides `2520`, so the least common multiple of
the digits seen so far can be represented by one of the divisors of `2520`.
Use digit DP with state `(position, remainder modulo 2520, lcm_state, tight)`.
Appending a digit updates the remainder and, for a nonzero digit, the LCM. At
the end, accept exactly when the remainder is divisible by that LCM. This state
is sufficient because future digits need only the current remainder and the
set-of-divisibility requirements compressed into their LCM. Count up to each
endpoint and subtract.

# 48. 840D -- Destiny

## Random sampling plus exact range counts

If a value appears more than `length / k` times, there can be fewer than `k`
such heavy values. Randomly sample several positions from the query range;
each heavy value has noticeable chance to be sampled. Pre-store sorted
occurrence positions for every value, so two binary searches verify a sampled
candidate's exact frequency. This is a randomized algorithm: the proof is a
failure-probability bound over independent samples, not a guarantee from one
sample. Always verify candidates; sampling alone can return a false answer.

# 49. 911G -- Mass Change Queries

## Push value transitions through a segment tree

Each node stores a mapping from every possible input value to its current
output value. A range operation replacing `x` by `y` composes this mapping at
covered nodes by redirecting outputs equal to `x`. Lazy composition means an
operation need not visit individual array positions. After all operations,
push mappings down to leaves and apply each leaf's mapping to its original
value. The invariant is functional composition: a node tag represents exactly
the sequence of replacements applied to its entire segment.

# 50. 1100F -- Ivan and Burgers

## Offline ranges with a position-aware xor basis

Sweep right endpoints. Maintain a linear basis of xor vectors, but attach to
each basis vector the latest array position needed to form it. When inserting a
new value, Gaussian-eliminate by highest bit and keep the representation with
the larger minimum position. For a query `[l,r]` answered at `r`, use only basis
vectors whose stored position is at least `l`; greedily add them when they
increase the xor. The position annotation is the invariant that makes one
global basis answer many left boundaries exactly.

# D. Ribbon Cuts (Offline Blind Capstone)

Official companion: <https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/189/A>

## Restatement and state

Use the ribbon exactly and maximize the number of pieces whose lengths belong
to `{a,b,c}`. Greedily taking the shortest length can leave an uncuttable
remainder, so record the best answer for every exact used length.

Let `dp[x]` be the maximum number of pieces that form total length `x`, or an
unreachable sentinel. Set `dp[0]=0`. For every `x` from one through `n`, append
any allowed cut `d` when `d <= x`:

```text
dp[x] = max(dp[x-d] + 1 for d in {a,b,c} with d <= x)
```

If `dp[n]` remains unreachable, output `-1`.

## Correctness proof

Every valid cutting of length `x` has a final piece of length `d`; removing it
leaves a valid cutting of `x-d`. By induction, `dp[x-d]` stores the largest
piece count for that remainder, so appending `d` considers the best cutting
with that final piece. Taking the maximum considers all possible final pieces.
Conversely every transition appends an allowed piece to an exact cutting, so it
is valid. Thus `dp[n]` is exactly the requested optimum, or unreachable.

## Complexity and tests

There are `n` states and three transitions per state: `O(n)` time and `O(n)`
memory. Test an impossible remainder, equal cut lengths, and a case where the
shortest cut is not part of an optimum. The local tiny oracle is a recursive
exact-cut search; the scale case has `n=200000`.

# Stress and carry-forward

For Gates 1--2, compare random small cases to brute force: enumerate windows,
paths, subsets, or point classifications. For Gates 3--4, first validate the
model on tiny instances: exhaustive dish orders, a brute MST, exact substring
sets, all triples, a direct range score, and a small flow implementation. The
reusable lesson is not the task name. It is the chain:

```text
statement signal -> state/invariant -> proof obligation -> update rule -> test
```
